newsitem.title: USA: Cisco acquisition drags down xDSL stocks.
newsitem.headline: Cisco acquisition drags down xDSL stocks.

text.p: Cisco Systems Inc's $125 million acquisition of high-speed networking business of Integrated Network Corp dragged down Cisco shares on Monday after the company said the purchase would damp near-term earnings.

The news also hit shares of niche players in the emerging market for high-speed Internet access over phone lines, which include companies such as Westell Technologies Inc and PairGain Technologies Inc, analysts said.
At midday, Cisco stock was off 15/16 to 78-3/4. Westell dropped 1-5/16 to 18-11/16. PairGain fell 13/16 to 21-1/8 and was among the most active Nasdaq issues.

Analysts said Cisco's latest acquisition reinforces its move into the high-speed data access business and raises the specter of futher consolidation in an industry that includes a score of competitors, many of them small start-ups.
Hambrecht & Quist analyst Farrokh Billimoria said the purchase would beef up Cisco's high-speed access products for small business, telecommuter and residential customers.
"It clearly re-emphasizes their push to become a full service provider to the (telephone) carrier market," Billimoria said.

Cisco's acqusition of Integrated Network Corp's Dagaz unit gives it access to digital subscriber line (DSL) technology that transmits high-speed data, video and voice service quickly and easily over ordinary telephone lines.

Westell is a leader in using similar technology in products aimed at residential customers, while PairGain leads among business customers who use DSL systems for high-speed data transmission or Internet access.

Most major U.S. phone carriers have announced plans to test and deploy DSL technology to provide high-speed Internet access to local service customers, but widescale deployment is still seen as several years away.
"This market is in a state of consolidation and preparation that should materalize over the next two or three years," UBS Securities analyst Nikos Teodosopoulous said.
"Cisco is doing like they do with any emerging technology," he said. "They are acquiring expertise and getting ready for the market to take off."
Billimoria and other analysts agreed that Cisco's move had sent a chill through stocks whose core business is in high-speed Internet access.
But Teodosopoulous argued that it was still to early to pick clear winners and losers in this market segment of the network-equipment supply business.

Earlier Monday, Cisco said it expected to take an after-tax charge of between $53.5 million and $73.6 million, $0.08 to $0.11 per share, in its fiscal first quarter ending in October to cover the costs of the acquisition.
But Cisco said it expected the transaction to have a neutral impact on its earnings in the first year and to add to profits thereafter.
